subject: Agriculture
title: The Columbian Exchange
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Columbian Exchange.

hook.text: Before Columbus, Europe had no potatoes, tomatoes, or corn. The Americas had no wheat, horses, or cattle.

buildup.text: After 1492, plants, animals, and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions—the Columbian Exchange.

discovery.text: Potatoes thrived in European soils and fed millions. Corn became Africa's staple. Global diets transformed.

twist.text: European diseases devastated Indigenous populations—killing up to 90% in some regions.

climax.text: The exchange reshaped global agriculture permanently. No continent farms the way it did before 1492.

punchline.text: Two hemispheres traded crops—and changed every plate on Earth.

quiz.question: Which crop from the Americas became a staple food in Europe after the Columbian Exchange?

details.summary: The Columbian Exchange was the massive transfer of plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and the Old World after 1492. This topic examines how crops like potatoes, corn, and tomatoes transformed global agriculture and diets forever.
details.whyItMatters: The Columbian Exchange reshaped every cuisine and food system on Earth. Foods now considered traditional in many countries—like Italian tomatoes or Irish potatoes—arrived only 500 years ago.
takeaways: Potatoes and corn from the Americas fueled European population growth
Old World wheat, cattle, and horses transformed the Americas
The exchange also brought devastating diseases that killed 90% of Indigenous populations

faq.question: What crops were transferred during the Columbian Exchange?
faq.answer: The Americas contributed corn, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco, peppers, squash, and beans to the Old World. Europe, Africa, and Asia contributed wheat, rice, sugarcane, coffee, cattle, horses, pigs, and chickens to the Americas.

faq.question: How did the Columbian Exchange change global agriculture?
faq.answer: It dramatically expanded the crop options available on every continent. Potatoes and corn boosted food production in Europe and Africa, while wheat and livestock transformed American farming. Global diets and agricultural systems were permanently reshaped.
